claims.text: A growing share of buy now pay later users are using the loans to cover everyday necessities like groceries, not just discretionary purchases
Splitting a purchase into smaller installment payments makes people more likely to buy an item and to spend more overall than they would if asked to pay the full price at once
A large share of buy now pay later users have missed or paid late on an installment in the past year
Buy now pay later loans are disproportionately originated to borrowers with subprime or lower credit scores
Pay-in-four buy now pay later loans charge the shopper no interest when paid on time, but the lender collects a fee of several percent of the sale from the merchant instead

A buy now pay later loan's advertised 0% interest does not mean the loan is free: the cost shows up through merchant fees embedded in prices, through late or overdraft fees, or through interest on longer-term plans
Buy now pay later's approval process typically relies on a soft credit check or no credit check at all, which makes it accessible to people who could not qualify for a traditional credit card
Buy now pay later is best suited to larger, planned purchases rather than small routine spending like fast food or groceries
A substantial share of buy now pay later users say they used the loans because it was the only way they could afford the purchase, not primarily for convenience or cash-flow management

The total amount of money outstanding in buy now pay later loans at any given time is small compared to total credit card or household debt, so a wave of defaults in this market alone is unlikely to trigger a broad financial crisis
Paying off a buy now pay later loan builds little to no lasting credit history because each pay-in-four loan closes once repaid instead of remaining open as a revolving line like a credit card
Longer-term buy now pay later installment loans often carry real interest rates comparable to or higher than credit cards, despite the brand's association with interest-free pay-in-four plans
Buy now pay later is structurally different from a credit card because it creates a new individual installment loan for each purchase instead of extending one revolving line of credit
A majority of buy now pay later users say they are unable to pay their monthly installments in full
Buy now pay later marketing, especially through social media and influencer content, normalized splitting everyday and discretionary purchases into installments for young consumers
A leading buy now pay later provider says its default rate is well below the industry average
A buy now pay later company's CEO says its model produces lower credit losses than a traditional credit card business during an economic downturn
A buy now pay later company's CEO says its average customer balance is small and turns over multiple times a year, unlike a credit card balance that can revolve for a long time
Buy now pay later companies as a group have struggled to turn a consistent profit despite rapid growth, because loan losses and the cost of funding loans often exceed what they earn in merchant fees
Buy now pay later companies can use detailed purchase data to target offers and marketing to consumers in ways banks have not

US regulatory oversight of buy now pay later weakened starting in 2025, after the CFPB's 2024 rule applying credit-card-style protections to these loans was withdrawn and the agency scaled back enforcement
Lenders and credit scoring models are moving toward reporting and counting buy now pay later loans, so a missed payment is increasingly likely to affect a user's credit report and score going forward
Most buy now pay later providers historically have not reported on-time payments to the major credit bureaus, so paying a loan off as agreed usually does not help build a user's credit score
A missed buy now pay later payment can hurt a user's credit score even when their on-time payments never helped it
Buy now pay later makes it easy for a user to stack multiple simultaneous loans across different apps that don't share data with each other, making total debt hard to track

Buy now pay later companies argue their short-term, small installment loans should be regulated differently from credit cards, while critics say the real motive is avoiding consumer-protection rules that already apply to credit cards
Heavy use of buy now pay later is linked to borrowers carrying bigger overall debt loads
Financing a purchase instead of saving up for it costs more in total once interest applies, even when marketed as a path to affordability
Buy now pay later companies market their product as fundamentally different from and friendlier than credit cards, while using a similar interest-based revenue model for their longer-term loans
Buy now pay later customers as a group are younger, spend more impulsively, and have more purchasing power than typical credit card users because of split payments

Using one buy now pay later loan to make a payment on a different debt, or paying a buy now pay later installment with a credit card, is a common way users extend how long they can delay actually paying for a purchase
Some buy now pay later lenders charge late fees as high as 25% of the total loan amount
Some buy now pay later lenders use detailed tracking of a user's location, app activity, and browsing history to target advertising and pricing
Black and Hispanic adults use buy now pay later at a notably higher rate than white adults, a gap that persists even after accounting for income and age
Lower-income buy now pay later users pay late far more often than higher-income users
Because buy now pay later payments are pulled automatically from a bank account on a fixed schedule, users are more likely to incur a separate overdraft or insufficient-funds fee from their own bank

Because buy now pay later loans are split across multiple apps and lenders that don't share data with each other, no single lender can see how much buy now pay later debt a borrower is carrying elsewhere

Buy now pay later's typical six-week repayment period creates problems for standard credit-reporting models, which can make opening several short loans in a short period look like a score-lowering event
Nearly half of buy now pay later users say they have experienced at least one financial problem with the service, most commonly overspending or a missed payment
Buy now pay later's growth has increasingly come from expanding beyond one-time retail purchases into recurring necessities like rent, groceries, gas, and utility bills
Rising use of buy now pay later for everyday essentials is widely read as a sign of a broader affordability crisis rather than simple consumer preference
An unpaid buy now pay later balance can be transferred to a debt collection agency after missed reminders
Buy now pay later lenders are setting aside unusually large loss reserves for loans they expect borrowers to never repay
Returning an item bought with buy now pay later is more complicated than returning a normal purchase because the loan balance must be separately adjusted once the merchant confirms the return
Buy now pay later's 'flypaper effect' increases how much people spend on small, lower-priced goods beyond what they would ordinarily buy
Buy now pay later debt is typically treated as ordinary unsecured consumer debt, the same legal category as credit card debt, and can usually be discharged in personal bankruptcy
Buy now pay later's typical four-payment structure was designed in a way that let it avoid disclosure requirements that apply to traditional credit under the Truth in Lending Act
Once a buy now pay later account is charged off, a creditor can obtain a court judgment and then freeze or seize money directly from the borrower's bank account through a levy

A lawsuit alleged that a major buy now pay later lender approves purchasing power without investigating a borrower's ability to repay, rather than underwriting each loan the way traditional lenders do
A major buy now pay later lender's credit-loss reserves spiked sharply after it went public, reflecting worsening repayment among its borrowers
A credit bureau study found that consumers who paid off their buy now pay later loans on time saw their FICO score rise an average of 13 points
Multiple buy now pay later transactions appear as separate tradelines on a credit report instead of one account, which some lenders could read as a sign of risky financial behavior
A buy now pay later company's CEO has publicly argued that credit card interest rates function as an extraction machine and backed a proposed cap on credit card interest rates

Because buy now pay later approval doesn't typically require a hard credit check or full income verification, it can let a borrower take on more installment debt than a traditional underwritten lender would extend
US regulators have investigated and moved to apply consumer-lending oversight to major buy now pay later companies due to concerns the loans could harm consumers
Buy now pay later approval is not guaranteed even for people who might expect to qualify; applications can be denied
Markets have reacted to new buy now pay later regulation by pricing in a hit to these companies' future profits and growth
Expanding buy now pay later lending to people who may not be able to repay it raises the same kind of credit-crisis risk regulators watch for when any form of consumer credit grows quickly
A buy now pay later pay-in-four loan paid entirely on time and in full costs the borrower exactly the item's sticker price, with no interest added
Splitting a purchase into smaller buy now pay later payments can give a budget more breathing room for other monthly expenses, compared to paying the full cost at once
Whether a buy now pay later loan is truly interest-free in practice depends on the borrower's credit profile, since some applicants are offered 0% while others are offered an interest-bearing rate
In the UK, some buy now pay later credit agreements appear on and affect a user's credit file, improving it with on-time payments and harming it with missed ones
Multiple credit checks from applying for buy now pay later credit within a short period can hurt a user's credit score
A county court judgment obtained against an unpaid buy now pay later debt has an even greater negative impact on a user's credit score than the missed payments alone

Buy now pay later's merchant fees are higher than standard credit card processing fees, which can push retailers toward raising prices that are then paid by all customers, including those who never use buy now pay later
Online retailers use buy now pay later partly to reduce shopping-cart abandonment, deploying it as a marketing and conversion tool rather than purely a financing option
Younger adults and people with lower or limited credit history make up a disproportionate share of BNPL users.
BNPL's instant, frictionless checkout encourages impulse purchases of items a buyer would not have bought if paying in full today.
Simulations of a new BNPL-inclusive credit-scoring approach found that most buy now pay later users see their credit score stay the same or rise slightly.
A large share of BNPL users carry multiple simultaneous loans across different providers at the same time.
A new FICO scoring model that factors in BNPL loans can raise or lower a user's credit score depending on their repayment history.
A BNPL purchase made shortly before filing bankruptcy can be challenged as non-dischargeable if a court finds it was made without any intent to repay.
Missing a BNPL payment can trigger late fees, account holds, or collections even though the loan itself carries no interest.
One of the top reasons people choose buy now pay later over a credit card is that it does not show up on a credit check.
Retailers accept higher processing fees for BNPL than for credit cards because it increases how many shoppers complete a purchase, not just how much they spend.
Using BNPL for a single large, planned, necessary purchase that already fits an existing budget is a reasonable use of the product.
Because most BNPL loans are not visible to lenders or credit bureaus, regulators cannot fully measure how much consumer debt they represent.
BNPL's rapid, loosely regulated growth mirrors conditions behind the 2008 subprime mortgage crisis, including extending credit to borrowers who may not be able to repay it.
A BNPL plan with zero stated interest can still trigger a bank overdraft or insufficient-funds fee if a scheduled installment arrives when the linked account balance is low.
Using BNPL to pay for recurring necessities like groceries or food delivery is a sign a household is financially stretched.
Truth in Lending Act protections like standardized billing-dispute and refund rules do not automatically apply to most BNPL pay-in-4 loans the way they apply to credit cards.
BNPL providers collect and sell data about users' shopping habits from checkout pages to other brands for marketing purposes.
Most buy now pay later users are already carrying debt on another credit card before they start using these services.
Budgeting for a BNPL plan the same way you would budget for a loan, rather than treating it as free money, avoids most of its risks.
Buy now pay later is a modern version of old layaway plans, except the customer receives the item immediately rather than after paying in full.
A BNPL provider's underwriting is built to protect its own loan portfolio from default, not primarily to protect the consumer from overspending.
Close to half of buy now pay later users report at least one problem such as overspending, a missed payment, or a regretted purchase.
Some buy now pay later installment plans now last longer and charge interest, making the industry behave more like traditional credit cards over time.
Most BNPL pay-in-4 loans are paid back in full and on time, and most users do not report serious problems with the service.
BNPL is marketed as safer than credit cards because it typically carries no compounding interest and cuts off users who miss a payment.
Taking out many buy now pay later loans in a short period is treated by credit-risk analysts as a signal of potential cash-flow problems, similar to other unsecured installment loans.
A majority of buy now pay later purchases processed through at least one major payments platform are net-new transactions rather than ones that would otherwise have gone on a credit card.
Buy now pay later transaction volume has been growing faster, in percentage terms, than other payment methods.
Company-reported default or late-fee rates for buy now pay later are far lower than independent consumer survey estimates of financial distress among users.

Financial apps that reward spending with points or cash-back features make overspending feel like a game, which increases how often people use the product and how likely they are to miss a payment or incur a fee.
Buy now pay later belongs to a broader category of apps — alongside gambling and crypto apps — that apply game-like design to financial products in order to increase how often people use them.
BNPL splits a purchase into equal installments over several weeks with no interest if every payment is made on time.
Buy now pay later firms typically fund the loan through a partner bank and then take ownership of the loan themselves, rather than lending their own money directly.
Major BNPL companies lose money on their interest-free loans and rely on other revenue lines to stay in business.
Klarna's longer-term financing option can charge a higher interest rate than a typical credit card, even though its short pay-in-4 plan is interest free.
Doom spending — splurging despite a bleak financial outlook — is made easier by apps like buy now pay later that make it simple to lose track of how much one is actually spending.
Young adults are turning to both credit cards and buy now pay later as wages fail to keep pace with the rising cost of living, deepening generational debt.
The average buy now pay later loan is small enough that even consistent on-time repayment is unlikely to significantly move a person's credit score.
A majority of BNPL users do not report a late payment or a BNPL-triggered bank fee in a given year.
Many buy now pay later users misunderstand whether using the service builds or protects their credit history.
Splitting a buy now pay later purchase into several smaller payments can make a person believe they can still afford the original purchase, even though the total cost hasn't changed.
Returns and refund disputes can be harder to resolve for a buy now pay later purchase than for one made with a credit card, because consumer protections for BNPL are inconsistent across providers.
Customer service for at least one major buy now pay later provider is difficult to escalate, making it hard to resolve a dispute over a purchase.
Paying off a buy now pay later loan early can trigger a prepayment penalty rather than saving the borrower money.
Carrying buy now pay later balances on a bank statement can hurt a mortgage application even though it isn't traditional credit
A purchase you can't pay for right now is one you can't actually afford, even split into installments
People struggling to pay essential bills like car insurance often still find money for discretionary buy now pay later purchases
Buy now pay later lenders cut off further credit to customers who always pay off balances early because that behavior isn't profitable for the lender
Buy now pay later debt is adding on top of already record-high US credit card debt rather than replacing it
Buy now pay later providers profit from merchants paying a transaction fee while also getting shoppers to spend more per cart than they would otherwise
A borrower with no significant income or assets can become 'judgment-proof,' making a buy now pay later lawsuit judgment effectively uncollectable
Buy now pay later providers raise a customer's available credit limit over time, encouraging them to borrow more
Fixed-term, interest-free installment loans like buy now pay later are a healthier form of credit than revolving credit cards
Removing late fees entirely leads buy now pay later customers to rack up more debt, because there's no consequence for paying late
Following a basic 50/30/20 budget split between needs, wants and savings is enough financial guidance for the average person
Using buy now pay later's interest-free pay-in-four option is fine as long as the money for each payment is already set aside
Buy now pay later's recurring per-purchase underwriting makes the business recession-proof compared to credit cards
A major buy now pay later provider can post large annual losses and cut a significant share of its workforce while still expanding into new markets
Buy now pay later providers don't let customers transfer balances or withdraw cash the way a credit card can, which limits how the debt can be misused
Big tech companies like Apple entering the buy now pay later market signals it is becoming a mainstream alternative to credit cards
Some buy now pay later providers focus on financing big-ticket purchases while others focus on everyday smaller purchases
Buy now pay later providers can aggregate a month of a customer's purchases into a single bill, letting merchants offer a cheaper payment option than standard card processing fees
Buy now pay later providers are expanding beyond installment loans into debit cards and neobank-style accounts
Buy now pay later providers compete for exclusive retailer partnerships, switching which company a large retailer like Walmart uses
Buy now pay later's individual per-transaction underwriting gives providers more control over how much debt a consumer can take on than a revolving credit card line does
Younger consumers using buy now pay later are more likely to fall into debt or miss a payment than older users
Spreading a purchase into buy now pay later installments protects a shopper if a financial hardship hits before they finish paying
Buy now pay later accounts often don't appear on a standard credit report, so they can be overlooked when filing for bankruptcy
Racking up new buy now pay later debt right after deciding to file for bankruptcy can be treated as bankruptcy fraud and risk denial of the discharge
In certain no-asset bankruptcy filings, a debt that wasn't listed on the petition can still get discharged automatically
